_readme: Each reference_gloss below was hand-derived from the four ISL properties
documented in gloss.py's own docstring (time/topic first, SOV order,
wh-signs last, negation after the verb, function words dropped) -- NOT by
running the code. That's the point: this set tests whether the rule-based
converter actually implements its own stated design, and separately
catches word-choice/tagger-dependent errors vs pure re-ordering errors.
'confidence' is how sure I am the reference matches what NLTK's
averaged_perceptron_tagger will actually assign, since I traced this by
hand without a live tagger (no network in this sandbox). 'high' = common,
unambiguous POS patterns. 'medium'/'low' = tagger-dependent edge cases
(bare interjections, isolated function words) where the tagger could
reasonably go a different way -- if eval_gloss.py disagrees on one of
those, check the actual tag before assuming the rule is wrong.
NONE of this validates ISL correctness itself -- these gloss orders are
still an approximation per the four documented rules, not checked against
ISLRTC materials or a signer. This only measures rule-implementation
fidelity and surfaces edge cases (see e.g. gloss_neg_bare, where 'No' as a
standalone word may get tagged DT and stripped before negation logic ever
sees it -- a real interaction bug worth checking).

cases.note: 'she'/'him'/'her' aren't in PRONOUNS, unlike i/me/my/you/your -- check whether that's an intentional gap.
No verb tag remains once 'is' is dropped, so nothing moves to clause-final position -- worth deciding if that's the intended behavior for predicate adjectives.

cases.text: The cat is on the table.
cases.note: Locative 'on' is dropped entirely -- spatial relation is lost, a known lossy simplification worth naming in the paper.
Modal-after-verb placement is this codebase's own choice, not one of the four documented properties -- flag for signer review before citing it as an ISL claim.
'him' isn't in PRONOUNS so it lemmatizes as a plain noun -- likely the same gap as sov_basic_2.
Yes/no questions have no wh-word to move, so the gloss ends up identical in shape to a plain statement -- question intent is lost. Worth naming as a limitation.
Matches the gloss you already saw render live in ar.html -- a known-good regression check.
Checks that negation is detected independently of the BE-drop path -- 'am' is dropped but 'not' still triggers NOT.
Compound case: contraction expansion + time-first + modal-final + negation all in one sentence.
Confirms sentences are glossed independently and concatenated, not merged across the boundary.

Deliberately adversarial: a bare 'No' may get tagged DT by NLTK, which is stripped in DROP_TAGS before the negation check ever runs on it -- likely produces [] instead of [NOT]. If eval_gloss.py shows exactly that, it's a real rule-interaction bug, not a bad reference.
